title: Tiger King
event_title: Tiger King is released on Netflix
lede: A Netflix documentary about big-cat owners, released in the first week of lockdown, followed from what viewers looked up to a federal law.
description: A time-ordered ripple map for Tiger King: each step dated and marked by how it was measured.
limits: Wikipedia stands in for all attention and one city's library for borrowing. Timing shows order, not proof that the event caused each step on its own.
dataline: Wikimedia pageviews (daily), Seattle Public Library checkouts (monthly), Congress (GovTrack)

steps.title: People borrow books on the exotic-animal trade
steps.heading: Wild animal trade
steps.note: Seattle's library was closed from April to August 2020.

steps.title: The House passes the Big Cat Public Safety Act
steps.measure: H.R. 1380, 116th Congress; the bill was introduced before the show
steps.note: The Senate did not take it up that session. Public record, not measured by us.

steps.title: On the House floor, a member cites Tiger King in the debate on the bill that became the law
steps.measure: the Congressional Record, Jul 28, 2022, page H7388
steps.note: Rep. Ed Case, in the debate on H.R. 263: the TV series “Tiger King” showed us that there is a dark and dangerous side to keeping lions, tigers, and other big cats in captivity. A citation shows the show was in the room when the law was made, not that it caused the law. Found by the engine in the Congressional Record.

steps.title: The Big Cat Public Safety Act becomes law
steps.note: Public record. The show is one of several forces behind the law; this map shows timing, not cause.
